stops.narrative: Inspect the counterweight. Separate its visible form, the museum’s functional interpretation and the unresolved relationship between object dating and regional chronology.
Read Makah accounts of cedar work, oral history and custody. The displayed photograph is later community documentation; the house-burial date remains disputed.
Find the work of coordinating a hunt and processing food. Keep a later landscape photograph and a limited cooking experiment distinct from an ancient event.
Investigate growing, storing and exchanging food beside hunting. Compare the village with Ozette: similar needs do not make the communities identical.
Begin with named people in a photograph, then read the community-led study of patterns, materials and language. Changing clothes need not mean an ended culture.
Separate a ban from the practice it targeted, and publication from community authority. Learn why 1980 is an institutional milestone, not the end of a people or of return efforts.

conclusion: Hunting, gardening, woodworking, sewing and witnessing drew on distinct systems of skill and responsibility. Material traces establish some facts; community accounts and careful source reading establish others. Similar needs never make these peoples interchangeable, and neither a relocation nor a legal prohibition proves that a culture ended.

evidence.prompt: Which comparison best respects both the material evidence and the community accounts?

options.text: Hidatsa gardens and Makah cedar work sustained different communities; material traces and community accounts answer complementary questions.
options.feedback: The community-authored subsistence guide documents Hidatsa garden/storage work. Makah sources explain cedar techniques and custody. These specific histories support comparison without proving identical institutions or direct contact.

options.text: A photograph of one Arctic outfit or one bison jump can describe how all northern peoples lived.
options.feedback: The photograph names particular people in dancing costume. Plains evidence includes village agriculture as well as communal hunting. Neither image supplies a universal regional identity.

options.text: Once a village moved or potlatching was banned, the people and their knowledge ceased to exist.
options.feedback: The MHA history traces relocation and continuity. U’mista documents potlatching during prohibition and community efforts to recover belongings. Administrative dates are not the lifespan of a people.
